title: حِكَايَةُ الْبَطَّةِ مَعَ الشِّبْلِ
titleEn: The Duck and the Lion Cub
part: Night 147 · The Duck and the Lion Cub ends / The Hermit and the Pigeons begins
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 724–726 (Night 147, continuing directly from nights-146), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 147 ends the duck's story. The peahen urges the frightened duck to stay on the island, where the Son of Adam never comes, and when a cloud of dust turns out to be only a gazelle, the three become friends and live together in safety. Then a ship that has lost its way anchors off the island; the sailors come ashore, the peahen flies off, the gazelle flees, and the duck, stunned, is caught, crying that caution is no help against fate. The peahen flies back to the gazelle, mourns the duck in two lines of verse, and is persuaded to stay; when the gazelle warns her against the Son of Adam, she tells him the duck died because she had neglected to praise God, for every creature God made praises Him; and the gazelle gives himself to praise without pause. A second short tale begins, of a hermit on a mountain and a pair of pigeons, and breaks off with the dawn. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّابِعَةُ وَالْأَرْبَعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sābiʿatu wa-al-arbaʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the seventh-and-forty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and forty-seventh night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الطَّاؤسَةَ لَمَّا سَمِعَتْ مِنَ الْبَطَّةِ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ تَعَجَّبَتْ مِنْهُ غَايَةَ الْعَجَبِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-ṭāʾūsata lammā samiʿat mina al-baṭṭati hādhā al-kalāma taʿajjabat minhu ghāyata al-ʿajabi
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the peahen, when she heard from the duck this speech, wondered at it the utmost of wonder.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the peahen heard these words from the duck, she marvelled at them beyond measure.
sentences.n: The sentence the last night broke off is taken up again. ghāyata al-ʿajabi, “the utmost of wonder”, an adverbial accusative: she wondered to the very limit.

sentences.t: وَقَٰلَتْ يَا أُخْتِى إِنَّكِ أَمِنْتِ مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ لِأَنَنَّا فِي جَزِيرَةٍ مِنْ جَزَٰئِرِ الْبَحْرِ لَيْسَ لِابْنِ آدَمَ فِيهَا مَسْلَكٌ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat yā ukhtī innaki aminti mini ibni Ādama li-annanā fī jazīratin min jazāʾiri al-baḥri laysa li-ibni Ādama fīhā maslakun
sentences.l: And she said: O my sister, indeed-you are-safe from the Son of Adam, because we (are) on an island of the islands of the sea; there-is-not for the Son of Adam in-it a way-of-passage.
sentences.i: And she said, “My sister, you are safe from the Son of Adam here, for we are on one of the islands of the sea, where the Son of Adam has no way in.
sentences.n: The print spells qālat without its alif, قلت, as it often does; the dagger alif supplies it. In لاننّا the print sets its shadda on the second nūn; the mark is kept where printed, but the word is li-annanā, “because we”. جزئر is the print's spelling of jazāʾir, “islands”, without the long alif; the dagger alif supplies it. maslak, “a path, a way through”.

sentences.t: فَاخْتَارِى الْمُقَامَ عِنْدَنَا إِلَى أَنْ يُسَهِّلَ اللَّهُ أَمْرَكِ وَأَمْرَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-ikhtārī al-muqāma ʿindanā ilā an yusahhila allāhu amraki wa-amranā
sentences.l: So choose the staying with us until God makes-easy your affair and our affair.
sentences.i: So choose to stay with us, until God eases your lot and ours.”
sentences.n: ikhtārī, feminine imperative of ikhtāra, “choose”, spelt with ى for final ي, as the print often does. al-muqām, “staying, sojourn”. yusahhilu allāhu amraki, “may God make your affair easy”, a common turn for a happy outcome.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ إِنِّي أَخَافُ أَنْ يَطْرُقَنِي طَارِقٌ وَالْقَضَاءُ لَايَنْفَكُّ عَنْهُ آبِقٌ
sentences.tr: qālat innī akhāfu an yaṭruqanī ṭāriqun wa-al-qaḍāʾu lā yanfakku ʿanhu ābiqun
sentences.l: She said: Indeed-I fear that a night-comer should come-upon-me, and the decree, there-does-not get-free from-it a runaway.
sentences.i: She said, “I fear that some visitor in the night may come upon me; and from fate no runaway ever breaks free.”
sentences.n: ṭaraqa, “to come by night, knock”; ṭāriq, “one who comes by night”, a sudden calamity. al-qaḍāʾ, “the decree”, what God has ordained. ābiq, “a runaway (slave)”. ṭāriq and ābiq rhyme, the sajʿ of a proverb. The print runs lā yanfakku together as لاينفك; the spacing is kept.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ اقْعُدِى عِنْدَنَا وَأَنْتِ مِثْلُنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālati uqʿudī ʿindanā wa-anti mithlunā
sentences.l: And she said: Sit (stay) with us, and you (are) like-us.
sentences.i: The peahen said, “Stay with us, for you are one of us.”
sentences.n: The print has اتعدى, a misprint for اقعدى, corrected here. uqʿudī, “sit, stay”: qaʿada is the everyday word for staying put, and the next words take it up, ḥattā qaʿadat. wa-anti mithlunā, a circumstantial clause, “when you are like us”: a bird among birds.

sentences.t: وَلَا زَالَتْ بِهَا حَتَّى قَعَدَتْ
sentences.tr: wa-lā zālat bihā ḥattā qaʿadat
sentences.l: And she did not cease at-her until she stayed.
sentences.i: And she kept on at her until she stayed.
sentences.n: lā zāla bi-, “not to leave off (pressing) someone”: the peahen kept urging her. lā with the past, for lam yazal, is common in this text.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ يَا أُخْتِي أَنْتِ تَعْلَمِينَ قِلَّةَ صَبْرِى وَلَوْلَا أَنِّي رَأَيْتُكِ هُنَا مَا كُنْتُ قَعَدْتُ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat yā ukhtī anti taʿlamīna qillata ṣabrī wa-lawlā annī raʾaytuki hunā mā kuntu qaʿadtu
sentences.l: And she said: O my sister, you know the scantness of my patience; and were-it-not that I saw you here, I would not have stayed.
sentences.i: And she said, “My sister, you know how little patience I have; had I not seen you here, I would never have stayed.”
sentences.n: The print has تعدت, a misprint for قعدت, corrected here. ṣabr, “patience, endurance”: she means she cannot bear to stay anywhere for long. lawlā annī …, “were it not that I …”, answered by mā kuntu qaʿadtu, “I would not have stayed”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الطَّاؤُوسَةُ إِنْ كَانَ عَلَى جَبِينِنَا شَيْءٌ نَسْتَوْفَاهُ وَإِنْ كَانَ دَنَا أَجَلُنَا فَمَنْ يُخَلِّصُنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-ṭāʾūsatu in kāna ʿalā jabīninā shayʾun nastawfāhu wa-in kāna danā ajalunā fa-man yukhalliṣunā
sentences.l: And the peahen said: If there is on our forehead a thing, we shall-receive-it-in-full; and if our appointed-term has drawn-near, then who will-rescue us?
sentences.i: The peahen said, “If something is written on our brows, we shall meet it to the full; and if our hour has drawn near, who can save us?
sentences.n: ʿalā jabīninā, “on our forehead”: what is written there is one's destiny. nastawfāhu stands for Classical nastawfīhi, “we receive it in full”, with ā for ī, a Middle Arabic form. ajal, “the appointed term”, the hour of death.

sentences.t: وَلَنْ تَمُوتَ نَفْسٌ حَتَّى تَسْتَوْفِىَ رِزْقَهَا وَأَجَلَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-lan tamūta nafsun ḥattā tastawfiya rizqahā wa-ajalahā
sentences.l: And a soul will-not die until it receives-in-full its provision and its term.
sentences.i: No soul dies before it has received its full share of provision and the whole of its span.”
sentences.n: A saying in the spirit of the hadith: each creature's livelihood and lifespan are fixed, and it must use up both. Here the verb is spelt with ى, tastawfiya.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَاهُمَا فِي هَذَا الْكَلَامِ إِذْ طَلَعَتْ عَلَيْهِمَا غَبْرَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā humā fī hādhā al-kalāmi idh ṭalaʿat ʿalayhimā ghabratun
sentences.l: And while they-two (were) in this talk, lo, there rose upon them a dust-cloud.
sentences.i: While they were talking so, a cloud of dust rose up before them.
sentences.n: The print runs baynamā and humā together as فبينماهما; the spacing is kept. ghabra, “dust, a dust-cloud”, usually raised by something approaching.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ صَاحَتِ الْبَطَّةُ وَنَزَلَتِ الْبَحْرَ وَقَالَتِ الْحَذَرَ الْحَذَرَوَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ مَفَرٌّ مِنَ الْقَضَاءِ وَالْقَدَرِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika ṣāḥati al-baṭṭatu wa-nazalati al-baḥra wa-qālati al-ḥadhara al-ḥadhara wa-in lam yakun mafarrun mina al-qaḍāʾi wa-al-qadari
sentences.l: And at that the duck cried-out, and went-down (into) the sea, and said: The caution, the caution! even if there is no escape from the decree and the destiny.
sentences.i: At that the duck cried out and took to the sea, saying, “Beware, beware! though there is no fleeing from what is decreed and destined.”
sentences.n: The print runs al-ḥadhara and wa-in together as الحذروان; the spacing is kept. al-ḥadhara al-ḥadhara, the accusative of warning, as in the last night. wa-in, “even if, although”. al-qaḍāʾ wa-al-qadar, “decree and destiny”, a fixed pair.

sentences.t: فَبَعْدَ سَاعَةٍ انْكَشَفَتِ الْغَبْرَةُ وَبَانَ مِنْ تَحْتِهَا ظَبْيٌ فَاطْمَأَنَّتِ الْبَطَّةُ وَالطَّاؤُوسَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-baʿda sāʿatin inkashafati al-ghabratu wa-bāna min taḥtihā ẓabyun fa-iṭmaʾannati al-baṭṭatu wa-al-ṭāʾūsatu
sentences.l: And after an hour the dust-cloud cleared-away, and there appeared from beneath it a gazelle; and the duck and the peahen grew-calm.
sentences.i: After a while the dust cleared, and out from under it came a gazelle; and the duck and the peahen were at ease.
sentences.n: sāʿa, “an hour”, here simply “a little while”. ẓaby, “gazelle”. The hamza in فاطمأنت is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لِلْبَطَّةِ يَا أُخْتِي إِنَّ الَّذِى نَظَرْتِ وَحَذِرْتِ مِنْهُ ظَبْيٌ وَهَاهُوَقَدْ أَقْبَلَ نَحْوَنَا
sentences.tr: thumma qālat li-al-baṭṭati yā ukhtī inna alladhī naẓarti wa-ḥadhirti minhu ẓabyun wa-hā huwa qad aqbala naḥwanā
sentences.l: Then she said to the duck: O my sister, the-one-which you saw and were-wary of-it (is) a gazelle, and here he (is), he has come toward us.
sentences.i: Then the peahen said to the duck, “My sister, what you saw and took fright at is only a gazelle, and here he comes toward us.
sentences.n: The speaker is the peahen. The print runs hā huwa and qad together as هاهوقد; the spacing is kept. hā huwa, “here he is”, with qad and a past verb: “here he is, come toward us”.

sentences.t: فَلَيْسَ عَلَيْنَا مِنْهُ بَأْسٌ لِأَنَّ الظَّبْيَ إِنَّمَا يَأْكُلُ الْحَشَايِشَ مِنْ نَبَاتِ الْأَرْضِ
sentences.tr: fa-laysa ʿalaynā minhu baʾsun li-anna al-ẓabya innamā yaʾkulu al-ḥashāyisha min nabāti al-arḍi
sentences.l: So there-is-not upon us from-him harm, because the gazelle only eats the grasses of the plants of the earth.
sentences.i: We have nothing to fear from him, for the gazelle eats nothing but the grasses that grow from the ground.
sentences.n: lā baʾsa, “no harm”; the hamza in بأس is the print's own. innamā, “only”. al-ḥashāyish, “grasses, herbage”, is the print's spelling of Classical ḥashāʾish, with yāʾ for hamza.

sentences.t: وَكَمَا أَنْتِ مِنْ جِنْسِ الطَّيْرِ هُوَالْآخَرُ مِنْ جِنْسِ الْوُحُوشِ
sentences.tr: wa-ka-mā anti min jinsi al-ṭayri huwa al-ākharu min jinsi al-wuḥūshi
sentences.l: And as you (are) of the kind of the birds, he-the-other (is) of the kind of the wild-beasts.
sentences.i: And just as you are of the race of birds, so he for his part is of the race of beasts.
sentences.n: The print runs huwa and al-ākhar together as هوالآخر; the spacing is kept. huwa al-ākhar, “he, the other”, the colloquial “he too, he for his part”. jins, “kind, race”.

sentences.t: فَاطْمَئِنِّي وَلَا تَهْتَمِّي فَإِنَّ الْهَمَّ يُنْحِلُ الْبَدَنَ
sentences.tr: fa-iṭmaʾinnī wa-lā tahtammī fa-inna al-hamma yunḥilu al-badana
sentences.l: So be-calm, and do-not be-troubled, for the care wastes the body.
sentences.i: So be at peace and do not fret, for worry wears the body thin.”
sentences.n: The shaddas on تهتمّي and الهمّ are the print's own. ihtamma, “to be anxious”, from hamm, “care, worry”; anḥala, “to make lean, emaciate”.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ تُتِمَّ الطَّاؤُوسَةُ كَلَامَهَا حَتَّى وَصَلَ الظَّبْيُ إِلَيْهِمَا يَسْتَظِلُّ تَحْتَ ظِلِّ الشَّجَرَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lam tutimma al-ṭāʾūsatu kalāmahā ḥattā waṣala al-ẓabyu ilayhimā yastaẓillu taḥta ẓilli al-shajarati
sentences.l: And the peahen had not finished her speech until the gazelle reached them, seeking-shade under the shade of the tree.
sentences.i: The peahen had hardly finished speaking when the gazelle reached them, looking for shade beneath the tree.
sentences.n: lam … ḥattā, “had not … before”: the second action overtakes the first. istaẓalla, “to seek shade, shelter in the shade”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى الطَّاؤُوسَةَ وَالْبَطَّةَ سَلَّمَ عَلَيْهِمَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā al-ṭāʾūsata wa-al-baṭṭata sallama ʿalayhimā
sentences.l: And when he saw the peahen and the duck, he greeted them.
sentences.n: The fatḥas on الطاؤوسةَ and البطةَ are the print's own, marking them as objects of raʾā. sallama ʿalā, “to give the greeting of peace to”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُمَا إِنِّي دَخَلْتُ إِلَى هَذِهِ الْجَزِيرَةِ الْيَوْمَ فَلَمْ أَرَ أَكْثَرَ مِنْهَا خِصْبًا وَلَا أَحْسَنَ مِنْهَا مَسْكَنًا
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahumā innī dakhaltu ilā hādhihi al-jazīrati al-yawma fa-lam ara akthara minhā khiṣban wa-lā aḥsana minhā maskanan
sentences.l: And he said to them: Indeed-I entered into this island today, and I have not seen (one) more than-it in fertility, nor finer than-it in dwelling-place.
sentences.i: And he said to them, “I came to this island today, and I have never seen a place more fertile, or a fairer place to live.”
sentences.n: lam ara, jussive of raʾā, “I have not seen”. khiṣban and maskanan are accusatives of specification: “more (in) fertility, finer (in) dwelling”; the two rhyme.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ دَعَاهُمَا لِمُرَافَقَتِهِ وَمُصَافَاتِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma daʿāhumā li-murāfaqatihi wa-muṣāfātihi
sentences.l: Then he invited them-two to his companionship and his sincere-friendship.
sentences.i: Then he invited the two of them to keep him company and be his true friends.
sentences.n: The subject is the gazelle. murāfaqa, “keeping company”, and muṣāfāt, “sincere friendship” (from ṣafā, “to be pure, clear”), are verbal nouns of the third form, the form of doing a thing with someone: the two share the pattern mufāʿala and chime.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتِ الْبَطَّةُ وَالطَّاؤُوسَةُ تَوَدُّدَهُ إِلَيْهِمَا أَقْبَلَتَا عَلَيْهِ وَرَغِبَتَا فِي عِشْرَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾati al-baṭṭatu wa-al-ṭāʾūsatu tawaddudahu ilayhimā aqbalatā ʿalayhi wa-raghibatā fī ʿishratihi
sentences.l: And when the duck and the peahen saw his making-himself-loved toward them-two, they-two turned-toward him and desired his companionship.
sentences.i: When the duck and the peahen saw how warmly he courted their friendship, they turned to him and gladly sought his company.
sentences.n: raʾat is singular, agreeing with the first of the two subjects, as a verb placed first may; aqbalatā and raghibatā, coming after, are dual. tawaddud, “showing affection, seeking love” (fifth form of wadda, “to love”). ʿishra, “close companionship, living together”. The hamza in رأت is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَتَصَادَقُوا وَتَحَالَفُوا عَلَى ذَلِكَ وَصَارَ مَبِيتُهُمْ وَاحِدًا وَمَأْكَلُهُمْ وَمَشْرَبُهُمْ سَوَاءً
sentences.tr: fa-taṣādaqū wa-taḥālafū ʿalā dhālika wa-ṣāra mabītuhum wāḥidan wa-maʾkaluhum wa-mashrabuhum sawāʾan
sentences.l: And they befriended-one-another and swore-alliance-one-to-another on that; and their night-lodging became one, and their eating and their drinking alike.
sentences.i: So they became friends and swore to it together; they slept in one place, and their food and drink were shared alike.
sentences.n: taṣādaqū, taḥālafū: sixth-form verbs of doing something to one another, “they made friends with each other, swore to each other”. The verbs are now plural, for the three of them. mabīt, maʾkal, mashrab, “place or act of passing the night, of eating, of drinking”: nouns of place and time. sawāʾ, “equal, the same”.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا آمِنِينَ أٓكِلِينَ شَارِبِينَ حَتَّى مَرَّتْ بِهِمْ سَفِينَةٌ كَانَتْ تَائِهَةً فِى الْبَحْرِ فَأَرْسَتْ قَرِيبًا مِنْهُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazālū āminīna ākilīna shāribīna ḥattā marrat bihim safīnatun kānat tāʾihatan fī al-baḥri fa-arsat qarīban minhum
sentences.l: And they did not cease (being) safe, eating, drinking, until a ship passed by them which was straying in the sea, and it cast-anchor near them.
sentences.i: So they lived on in safety, eating and drinking, until a ship that had lost its way at sea passed by them and dropped anchor close at hand.
sentences.n: āminīn, ākilīn, shāribīn, “safe, eating, drinking”: three participles in a row, a recurring formula of the carefree life. The print writes أكلين with a plain hamza for آكلين, ākilīn; the madda is supplied in the pointing. tāʾih, “lost, wandering astray”. arsā, “to cast anchor” (of a ship, arsat): فارست is fa-arsat, “and it anchored”, not a misprint. marrat bihim, “passed by them”: marra takes bi-.

sentences.t: فَطَلَعَ النَّاسُ وَتَفَرَّقُوا فِى الْجَزِيرَةِ فَرَأَوْا اجْتِمَاعَ الظَّبْيِ وَالطَّاؤُوسَةِ وَالْبَطَّةِ فَأَقْبَلُوا عَلَيْهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-ṭalaʿa al-nāsu wa-tafarraqū fī al-jazīrati fa-raʾaw ijtimāʿa al-ẓabyi wa-al-ṭāʾūsati wa-al-baṭṭati fa-aqbalū ʿalayhim
sentences.l: And the people came-up (ashore) and scattered in the island, and they saw the gathering-together of the gazelle and the peahen and the duck, and they came-toward them.
sentences.i: The people came ashore and spread out over the island, and they saw the gazelle, the peahen and the duck together, and made toward them.
sentences.n: ṭalaʿa, “to go up”, here “to land, come ashore” from the ship. ijtimāʿ, “being together”: they saw the three in company.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْهُمُ الطَّاؤُوسَةُ صَعِدَتْ إِلَى الشَّجَرَةِ ثُمَّ طَارَتْ فِى الْجَوِّ وَشَرَدَ الظَّبْيُ فِى الْبَرِّيَّةِ فَبَقِيَتِ الْبَطَّةُ مُخَبَّلَةً
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾathumu al-ṭāʾūsatu ṣaʿidat ilā al-shajarati thumma ṭārat fī al-jawwi wa-sharada al-ẓabyu fī al-barriyyati fa-baqiyati al-baṭṭatu mukhabbalatan
sentences.l: And when the peahen saw them, she went-up to the tree, then flew into the air; and the gazelle fled-off into the open-country; and the duck remained bewildered.
sentences.i: When the peahen saw them she went up into the tree and then flew off into the sky, and the gazelle bolted into the wilds; but the duck was left there, dazed and helpless.
sentences.n: sharada, “to run away, bolt”, of a frightened animal. barriyya, “open country, desert”. mukhabbala, “confused, dazed”, from khabal, “derangement”: she did not know which way to turn. The shadda on الجوّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا بِهَا حَتَّى صَادُوهَا
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazālū bihā ḥattā ṣādūhā
sentences.l: And they did not cease at her until they caught her.
sentences.i: They kept after her until they caught her.
sentences.n: The print has وام, a misprint for ولم, corrected here. lam yazālū bihā, “they did not leave off with her”: they kept at her. ṣāda, “to hunt, catch (game)”.

sentences.t: وَصَاحَتْ قَائِلَةً لَمْ يَنْفَعْنِى الْحَذَرُ مِنَ الْقَضَاءِ وَالْقَدَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāḥat qāʾilatan lam yanfaʿnī al-ḥadharu mina al-qaḍāʾi wa-al-qadari
sentences.l: And she cried-out, saying: Caution did not avail me against the decree and the destiny.
sentences.i: And she cried out, “Caution has not saved me from what God decreed and destined.”
sentences.n: al-qaḍāʾ wa-al-qadar, “the decree and the destiny”, God's ordaining of all that befalls; a pair that recurs through the tale, here rhyming ḥadhar with qadar. Compare the cub's tale, where fate struck and caution was no use.

sentences.t: وَانْصَرَفُوا بِهَا إِلَى سَفِينَتِهِمْ
sentences.tr: wa-inṣarafū bihā ilā safīnatihim
sentences.l: And they went-off with her to their ship.
sentences.i: And they carried her off to their ship.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتِ الطَّاؤُوسَةُ مَا جَرَي لِلْبَطَّةِ ارْتَحَلَتْ مِنَ الْجَزِيرَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾati al-ṭāʾūsatu mā jarā li-al-baṭṭati irtaḥalat mina al-jazīrati
sentences.l: And when the peahen saw what had befallen the duck, she departed from the island.
sentences.i: When the peahen saw what had happened to the duck, she left the island.
sentences.n: jarā li-, “to happen to”; the print writes جري with a dotted yāʾ for جرى; the spelling is kept. irtaḥala, “to set out, move away”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَا أَرَى الْآفَاتِ إِلاّ مُرَاصِدَةً لِكُلِّ أَحَدٍ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lā arā al-āfāti illā murāṣidatan li-kulli aḥadin
sentences.l: And she said: I do not see the calamities except lying-in-wait for every one.
sentences.i: And she said, “I see that misfortunes lie in wait for everyone.
sentences.n: āfa, “bane, calamity”. murāṣida, “watching for, lying in ambush for”. lā … illā, “not … except”: “I see calamities only as lying in wait”. The print sets its shadda over the alif of الاّ; it belongs to the lām, illā.

sentences.t: وَلَوْلَا هَذِهِ السَّفِينَةُ مَا حَصَلَ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ هَذِهِ الْبَطَّةِ افْتِرَاقٌ
sentences.tr: wa-lawlā hādhihi al-safīnatu mā ḥaṣala baynī wa-bayna hādhihi al-baṭṭati iftirāqun
sentences.l: And were-it-not-for this ship, there would not have come-about between me and this duck a parting.
sentences.i: Had it not been for this ship, there would never have been a parting between me and this duck.
sentences.n: lawlā, “were it not for”, is followed by a plain noun, and the answer comes with mā and the past tense: “there would not have happened”. ḥaṣala, “to come about, occur”.

sentences.t: وَلَقَدْ كَانَتْ مِنْ خِيَارِ الْأَصْدِقَاءِ
sentences.tr: wa-la-qad kānat min khiyāri al-aṣdiqāʾi
sentences.l: And truly she was of the choicest of the friends.
sentences.i: She was truly one of the best of friends.”
sentences.n: la-qad, “truly, indeed”, strengthens the past tense. khiyār, “the best, the pick”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ طَارَتِ الطَّاؤُوسَةُ وَاجْتَمَعَتْ بِالظَّبْيِ فَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهَا وَهَنَّاهَا بِالسَّلَامَةِ
sentences.tr: thumma ṭārati al-ṭāʾūsatu wa-ijtamaʿat bi-al-ẓabyi fa-sallama ʿalayhā wa-hannāhā bi-al-salāmati
sentences.l: Then the peahen flew and met with the gazelle, and he greeted her and congratulated her on the safety.
sentences.i: Then the peahen flew off and joined the gazelle, who greeted her and gave her joy of her safe escape.
sentences.n: ijtamaʿa bi-, “to meet with, join”: the verb takes bi-. sallama ʿalā, “to greet (with al-salām ʿalaykum)”. hannāhā, “he congratulated her”, for Classical hannaʾahā: the hamza has become a long vowel, as in speech. The shadda on هنّاها is the print's own. Note salām in sallama and salāma, “safety”: the greeting and the escape share a root.

sentences.t: وَسَأَلَهَا عَنِ الْبَطَّةِ
sentences.tr: wa-saʾalahā ʿani al-baṭṭati
sentences.l: And he asked her about the duck.
sentences.n: The hamza in سألها is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ قَدْ أَخَذَهَا الْعَدُوُّ وَكَرِهْتُ الْمُقَامَ فِي تِلْكَ الْجَزِيرَةِ بَعْدَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu qad akhadhahā al-ʿaduwwu wa-karihtu al-muqāma fī tilka al-jazīrati baʿdahā
sentences.l: And she said to him: The enemy has taken her, and I have-come-to-hate the staying in that island after her.
sentences.i: She said to him, “The enemy has taken her, and I could not bear to stay on that island once she was gone.”
sentences.n: al-ʿaduww, “the enemy”: man, as the animals see him. muqām, “staying, abode”. baʿdahā, “after her”, that is, without her. The shadda on العدوّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَكَتْ عَلَى فِرَاقِ الْبَطَّةِ وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ
sentences.tr: thumma bakat ʿalā firāqi al-baṭṭati wa-anshadat taqūlu
sentences.l: Then she wept over the parting-from the duck, and recited, saying:
sentences.i: Then she wept for the loss of the duck and recited this verse:
sentences.n: anshada, “to recite (verse)”, followed by taqūlu, “saying”, the stock lead-in to a poem.

sentences.t: اِنَّ يَوْمَ الْفِرَاقِ قَطَّعَ قَلْبِيْ * قَطَّعَ اللّهُ قَلْبَ يَوْم الْفِرَاقِ
sentences.tr: inna yawma al-firāqi qaṭṭaʿa qalbī * qaṭṭaʿa allāhu qalba yawmi al-firāqi
sentences.l: Indeed the day of parting has cut-to-pieces my heart; * may God cut-to-pieces the heart of the day of parting!
sentences.i: The day of parting has torn my heart to pieces; * may God tear to pieces the heart of the day of parting!
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own. qaṭṭaʿa, “to cut up, sever”, the second form for doing a thing thoroughly; the second hemistich turns the same verb into a curse. The print leaves يوم without its case vowel in the second half; it is read yawmi, governed by qalba.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ أَيْضًا هَذَا الْبَيْتَ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat ayḍan hādhā al-bayta
sentences.l: Then she said also this verse:
sentences.i: Then she recited this line as well:
sentences.n: bayt, “house”, is also a line of verse, two hemistichs long.

sentences.t: تَمَنَّيْتُ الْوِصَالَ يَعُودُ يَوْمًا * لِاُخْبِرُهُ بِمَا صَنَعَ الْفرَاقُ
sentences.tr: tamannaytu al-wiṣāla yaʿūdu yawman * li-ukhbiruhu bi-mā ṣanaʿa al-firāqu
sentences.l: I wished (that) the union might-return one day, * that I might tell it of what the parting has done.
sentences.i: I have longed for our union to come back one day, * so I might tell it all that parting has done.
sentences.n: The pointing is the print's own. wiṣāl, “union, being together”, the lover's word, opposite of firāq, “parting”. The print points لاخبره with a damma, li-ukhbiruhu; after li- of purpose Classical Arabic has the subjunctive, li-ukhbirahu.

sentences.t: فَاغْتَمَّ الظَّبْيُ غَمًّا شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: fa-ightamma al-ẓabyu ghamman shadīdan
sentences.l: And the gazelle grieved a severe grief.
sentences.i: The gazelle was deeply grieved.
sentences.n: ightamma … ghamman, “grieved a grief”: an absolute object from the same root, strengthened by shadīdan.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَدَّ عَزْمَ الطَّاؤُوسَةِ عَنِ الرَّحِيلِ
sentences.tr: thumma radda ʿazma al-ṭāʾūsati ʿani al-raḥīli
sentences.l: Then he turned-back the peahen's resolve from the departing.
sentences.i: Then he talked the peahen out of her resolve to leave.
sentences.n: ʿazm, “resolve, firm intention”. radda … ʿan, “to turn (something) away from”.

sentences.t: فَأَقَامَتْ مَعَ الظَّبْيِ آمَنِينَ آكَلِينَ شَارِبِينَ غَيْرَ أَنَّهُمَا لَمْ يَزَالَا حَزِينَيْنِ عَلَى فِرَاقِ الْبَطَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-aqāmat maʿa al-ẓabyi āminīna ākilīna shāribīna ghayra annahumā lam yazālā ḥazīnayni ʿalā firāqi al-baṭṭati
sentences.l: And she stayed with the gazelle, safe, eating, drinking, except that they-two did not cease (being) sad over the parting-from the duck.
sentences.i: So she stayed with the gazelle, and they lived in safety, eating and drinking, except that both of them grieved still for the loss of the duck.
sentences.n: The three participles are plural, āminīn …, though only two are left; the dual returns with lam yazālā ḥazīnayni. The print points آمَنين and آكَلين with a fatḥa on the second letter, which would read āmanīn, ākalīn; the fatḥas are the print's and are kept, but the words are the same āminīn, ākilīn of before. The fatḥa in حزينَين, marking the dual ḥazīnayni, is also the print's.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الظَّبْيُ لِلطَّاؤُوسَةِ يَا أُخْتِي قَدْ عَلِمْتِ أَنَّ النَّاسَ الَّذِينَ طَلَعُوا لَنَا مِنَ الْمَرْكَبِ كَانُوا سَبَبًا لِفِرَاقِنَا وَلِهَلَاكِ الْبَطَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ẓabyu li-al-ṭāʾūsati yā ukhtī qad ʿalimti anna al-nāsa alladhīna ṭalaʿū lanā mina al-markabi kānū sababan li-firāqinā wa-li-halāki al-baṭṭati
sentences.l: And the gazelle said to the peahen: O my sister, you have known that the people who came-up to us from the ship were a cause for our parting and for the perishing of the duck.
sentences.i: The gazelle said to the peahen, “My sister, you know that the people who came ashore upon us from the ship were the cause of our parting and of the duck's destruction.
sentences.n: Here the print writes الطاووسة with a plain wāw and a damma, without the hamza seat it uses elsewhere; the damma is the print's own and the hamza is supplied. markab, “ship”, a synonym of safīna. sabab li-, “a cause of”.

sentences.t: فَاحْذَرِيهِمْ وَاحْتَرِسِي مِنْهُمْ وَمِنْ مَكْرِ بَنِي آدَمَ وَخِدَاعِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-iḥdharīhim wa-iḥtarisī minhum wa-min makri banī Ādama wa-khidāʿihi
sentences.l: So beware-of them, and guard-yourself from them and from the cunning of the sons of Adam and his deceit.
sentences.i: So beware of them, and be on your guard against them and against the cunning and deceit of the sons of Adam.”
sentences.n: Feminine imperatives, iḥdharī and iḥtarisī, to the peahen. khidāʿihi, “his deceit”: the pronoun is singular, as if for ibn Ādam, man, though banī Ādam is plural.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ قَدْ عَلِمْتُ يَقِينًا أَنْ مَاقَتَلَهَا غَيْرُ تَرْكِهَا التَّسْبِيحَ
sentences.tr: qālat qad ʿalimtu yaqīnan an mā qatalahā ghayru tarkihā al-tasbīḥa
sentences.l: She said: I have known for-certain that naught killed her but her leaving-off the glorification (of God).
sentences.i: She said, “I know for certain that nothing killed her but her neglect of praising God.
sentences.n: The print runs ما قتلها together as ماقتلها; the spacing is kept. an, the lightened form of anna, introduces a negative clause: “that nothing killed her except”. tasbīḥ, “glorifying God”, saying subḥāna allāh; the tale's lesson is that every creature lives by praising its Maker.

sentences.t: وَلَقَدْ قُلْتُ لَهَا إِنِّي أَخَافُ عَلَيْكِ مِنْ تَرْكِكِ التَّسْبِيحَ لِأَنَّ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقَهُ اللَّهُ يُسَبِّحُهُ فَإِنْ غَفَلَ عَنِ التَّسْبِيحِ عُوقِبَ بِهَلَاكِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-la-qad qultu lahā innī akhāfu ʿalayki min tarkiki al-tasbīḥa li-anna kulla shayʾin khalaqahu allāhu yusabbiḥuhu fa-in ghafala ʿani al-tasbīḥi ʿūqiba bi-halākihi
sentences.l: And I did say to her: Indeed-I fear for you from your leaving-off the glorification; because every thing (that) God created, it glorifies Him, and if it neglects the glorification, it is punished with its perishing.
sentences.i: Indeed I told her, ‘I fear for you, because you have given up praising God; for every thing that God has made praises Him, and if it grows careless of His praise, it is punished with its own destruction.’”
sentences.n: khāfa ʿalā, “to fear for (someone)”. kullu shayʾin khalaqahu allāhu yusabbiḥuhu, “every thing God created glorifies Him”: an echo of the Qurʾānic teaching that all creation glorifies God. ʿūqiba, passive, “it is punished”. The shadda on يسبّحه is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الظَّبْيُ كَلَامَ الطَّاؤُوسَةِ قَالَ أَحْسَنَ اللَّهُ صُورَتَكِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-ẓabyu kalāma al-ṭāʾūsati qāla aḥsana allāhu ṣūrataki
sentences.l: And when the gazelle heard the speech of the peahen, he said: May God make-beautiful your form!
sentences.i: When the gazelle heard the peahen's words, he said, “May God make your form beautiful!”
sentences.n: aḥsana allāhu ṣūrataki, a blessing in the past tense, “may God make fair your form”, a fitting wish for a peahen; the past tense of a verb is the usual form of a prayer.

sentences.t: وَأَقْبَلَ عَلَى التَّسْبِيحِ لَا يَفْتُرُ عَنْهُ سَاعَةً
sentences.tr: wa-aqbala ʿalā al-tasbīḥi lā yafturu ʿanhu sāʿatan
sentences.l: And he turned-to the glorification, not slackening from it an hour.
sentences.i: And he gave himself to praising God, never slackening for a moment.
sentences.n: aqbala ʿalā, “to turn to, devote oneself to”. fatara ʿan, “to slacken, flag in”. sāʿa, “hour”, also “a moment, a while”.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ قِيلَ إِنَّ تَسْبِيحَ الظَّبْيِ سُبْحَانَ الدَّيَّانِ ذِى الْجَبَرُوتِ وَالسُّلْطَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad qīla inna tasbīḥa al-ẓabyi subḥāna al-dayyāni dhī al-jabarūti wa-al-sulṭāni
sentences.l: And it has been said that the glorification of the gazelle (is): Glory to the Judge, Possessor of the might and the dominion!
sentences.i: It is said that the gazelle's praise is: Glory be to the Judge of all, Lord of might and dominion!
sentences.n: The print has وقل, a misprint for وقد, corrected here. Each creature is given its own formula of praise, a common theme in pious lore. al-dayyān, “the Requiter, the Judge”, one of God's names; jabarūt, “overwhelming might”; sulṭān, “dominion”. dayyān and sulṭān rhyme. The shadda on الديّان is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَوَرَدَ أَنَّ بَعْضَ الْعُبَّادِ كَانَ يَتَعَبَّدُ فِي بَعْضِ الْجِبَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-warada anna baʿḍa al-ʿubbādi kāna yataʿabbadu fī baʿḍi al-jibāli
sentences.l: And it has come-down that one of the worshippers used-to devote-himself-to-worship in one of the mountains.
sentences.i: It is reported that a certain hermit used to devote himself to worship on a mountain.
sentences.n: A new tale begins, of the hermit and the pigeons. warada, “to arrive”, here “it is handed down, reported”, a formula for introducing a story. ʿubbād (sing. ʿābid), “worshippers, devotees”: men who withdraw to pray. baʿḍ … baʿḍ, “one of … one of”: “a certain hermit, on a certain mountain”. The shadda on العبّاد is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ يَأْوِي إِلَى ذَلِكَ الْجَبَلِ زَوْجٌ مِنَ الْحَمَامِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna yaʾwī ilā dhālika al-jabali zawjun mina al-ḥamāmi
sentences.l: And there used-to take-shelter in that mountain a pair of the pigeons.
sentences.i: On that same mountain there lived a pair of pigeons.
sentences.n: zawj, “one of a pair”, and also “a pair”, as here: a male and his mate. ḥamām, “pigeons, doves”, a collective noun. The hamza in يأوي is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ الْعَابِدُ قَسَمَ قُوتَهُ نِصْفَيْنِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna dhālika al-ʿābidu qasama qūtahu niṣfayni
sentences.l: And that worshipper had divided his sustenance (into) two halves —
sentences.i: That hermit used to divide his food into two halves —
sentences.n: The sentence breaks off here, cut by the dawn; the next night takes it up. qūt, “food, sustenance, what keeps one alive”. kāna with a past verb, kāna … qasama, usually “he had divided”; here the sense is probably habitual.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahr Zāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she ceased the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: Here the print sets Shahrazād's name as two words, شهر زاد; the spacing is kept.
